title: The 5 Things Managers Watch For Before Naming a Lead (It's Not Your Code)
author: Colette Molteni
summary: Colette Molteni, a 12-year analytics professional, argues that technical professionals who keep getting passed over for a lead role are being judged on five criteria that never appear in the job description. Managers file these under vague "soft skills" labels, which lets them justify promotion decisions without solid criteria, even though the capacities involved can be specific and structured. The five signals are moving before being told to move, questioning the spec before shipping it, listening to understand rather than to reply, staying steady when an incident hits, and hearing what was not said in the meeting. She illustrates each with a concrete workplace scene, such as a senior director's polite request to "double-check the timeline" that really hardens a deadline. Her broader claim is that as AI takes over more coding and drafting, this human layer of leadership becomes more valuable, and that nobody will hand you a checklist for it. The piece ends with a pitch for her one-on-one coaching, but the argument stands on its own.
points: Promotion to lead is decided less by technical output than by five largely unwritten signals, so being the best coder is not the same as being read as ready.

The "soft skills" label is a convenient vagueness that lets evaluators defend decisions, when the underlying behaviors (initiative, questioning, listening, composure, reading people) can be made exact and practiced.
Questioning a request before shipping it, rather than building exactly what was asked, is treated as the real meaning of "critical thinking" in a lead.
A lead acts as the team's shock absorber: calm and focused during an incident rather than amplifying the alarm.
Because AI is absorbing more technical drafting and coding, the human layer of leading (translating what is said into what it means) is the part that grows in value.
quotes: The lead is the person who sees the gap and closes it. Ambiguity is not a show-stopper. They clarify where they can, and move.
The person who jumps right to their point without acknowledgment isn’t leading the way. The person who listens, clarifies, or even challenges where applicable is leading the way.
The lead is the team’s shock absorber. You are the steady and stoic presence.
When a senior director says, “I am pleased with the direction, can you just double-check the timeline?”, can you tell the soft deadline has now hardened?
The lead translates what is said into what it means. They empathize. It is not always directly stated. Often, it isn’t, especially with non-technical folks.
The “soft skills” label makes it easy for evaluators to defend their decisions. When, really, most of these skills can be exact and structured.
The five capacities above are not the ones a model can do for you.
No manager is going to hand you a direct checklist of the things for you to do. If you wait for them, the next promotion cycle will pass.
